Revise the plan@1 at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gabe-Projects-callisto/ae412d01-e061-4047-918b-0d1df3d4d118/scratchpad/plan-manifest-persist-001.json (read it first) implementing .claude/specs/SPEC-MANIFEST-PERSIST-001.json (workspace root /Users/gabe/Projects/callisto). This is revision round 2 — a fresh, independent vector-challenger pass found 10 issues (3 blocking). Read every cited file yourself before writing any fix; verify claims, don't just apply suggested text blindly if the underlying code doesn't back it up.

Fix these findings (verbatim from the challenger):

1. **(BLOCKING) T19 has a fabricated red phase**: T19 is excluded from `red_phase_waived_tasks` and claims a genuine red phase ("before this file exists, `cargo test --test apply_persist_open_count_test` fails with a real, distinct cargo error... unlike T14-T18's case"). This is wrong — a missing cargo target is a build-configuration artifact, not evidence the assertion can fail for the right reason. `callisto_manifests::open_call_count() == 2` is invariant across this whole spec (the spec's non_goals item 1 says open/persist counts don't change; verify `apply_version_plan` has exactly two `open(&decl, &ctx)` call sites, in `crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs`, both before and after this refactor). The test passes on first execution. FIX: add "T19" to `red_phase_waived_tasks`, rewrite its `expected_failure` in the same honest form as T14-T18 ("NO RED PHASE -- AC-009 check (c) locks in an invariant this spec explicitly does not change per non_goals item 1; the test passes on first run. The 'no test target' error is a target-resolution artifact of the file not existing yet, not a red phase. Red-phase gate is explicitly waived."), and delete any sentence in T19's `reasoning` claiming otherwise.

2. **(BLOCKING) Six `expected_pass` test counts are fabricated for npm.rs/python.rs**: Read `crates/callisto-manifests/src/npm.rs`'s `mod tests` (starts ~line 459) and count the `#[test]` functions yourself — the challenger found 29 today, all in one module, no proptest! block. T07/T08/T09's `expected_pass` currently state 20/21/22 passed, implying a 19-test baseline that doesn't exist. Read `crates/callisto-manifests/src/python.rs`'s `mod tests` (starts ~line 587) and count its `#[test]` functions yourself — the challenger found 30. T10/T11/T12's `expected_pass` currently state 25/27/28, implying a 24-test baseline that doesn't exist. (Note: the challenger confirmed cargo.rs's counts — 21 baseline, 22/23/24 in T04/T05/T06 — are CORRECT; only npm/python are wrong.) FIX: count both files' test functions yourself precisely (don't just trust the challenger's 29/30 — recount, since a miscount here is exactly the kind of error that keeps recurring in this plan's history), then correct T07/T08/T09's and T10/T11/T12's `expected_pass` values to the correct baseline+N sequence. Consider whether exact counts are even the right verification mechanism here — if you'd rather express these as "0 failed, N new passing tests added to the existing suite" instead of a brittle absolute count, that's an acceptable alternative fix; pick whichever is more robust and correct it consistently.

3. **(BLOCKING) AC-009 check (b) — byte-identity assertion — has no implementing task**: AC-009 requires (per the spec) that "running apply_version_plan end-to-end produces the same on-disk bytes for every touched manifest path as the equivalent direct mutator-then-persist sequence asserted in AC-002/AC-003." T02/T03 currently only assert substring presence (`on_disk.contains("version = \"1.1.0\"")`), not byte-identity against a direct sequence; T19 covers only check (c) (open-count). FIX: add a step (to T03, or a new task after T13 — your choice, whichever fits the sequencing better) that, for one Cargo fixture and one PackageJson fixture: runs `apply_version_plan` on a single-bump plan and captures the resulting file bytes; then, in the same test, re-creates the identical starting fixture and performs the equivalent direct `open() -> write_version() -> persist()` sequence by hand; then asserts `assert_eq!` on the two full file contents (not `.contains()`). Add that task's id to AC-009's coverage in whichever task(s) claim it.

4. **T06 (the `ManifestError::InvariantViolation` self-delegation guard) should land before T03, not after**: T03 adds an unconditional `handle.persist(permit)?` to apply.rs's rewrites loop, but currently T06 (which adds the guard to `CargoToml::update_dependency_spec` preventing the exact silent-data-loss case this persist call could otherwise cause) doesn't land until 3 commits later. Read `crates/callisto-manifests/src/cargo.rs` lines ~303-307 (the delegation branch) yourself to confirm: for the self-referential case (handle's own path equals `self.workspace_root.join("Cargo.toml")`), an unconditional persist in T03 without T06's guard already in place would silently revert the delegation's write during the window between T03 and T06 landing — narrow (per AC-017, unreachable from real cascade.rs-produced plans) but real, and the plan currently claims this reordering is "provably harmless" which is false for this specific branch. FIX: reorder so T06 lands immediately after T01a/T01b and before T02/T03 (T06's own red phase is a compile error for the missing `InvariantViolation` variant, independent of any stripping task, so it can move freely). Update the task sequence and any task numbering/dependency references accordingly. Correct T03's `reasoning` to drop the "provably harmless" claim and instead state that T06's guard (already landed) makes this branch return `Err` before persist would ever be reachable for the self-referential case.

5. **T20 omits 3 of 7 `just ci` phases and is too large for one task**: Read the actual `justfile` at the workspace root, specifically the `ci:` recipe (~line 86: `ci: fmt-check lint test audit doc-check wasm-check coverage`) — 7 phases. T20 currently only enumerates 4 (fmt-check, lint/clippy, test, wasm-check), omitting `audit`, `doc-check`, and `coverage` entirely. `coverage` in particular runs under `--all-features` (check exactly what flags via the justfile), which compiles `callisto-manifests` with additional feature flags this plan never analyzed — a configuration where a newly-required trait method (`Manifest::persist`) is most likely to surface an unimplemented impl if one was missed. FIX: split T20 into per-phase verification steps (one sub-step per `just ci` phase, in justfile order) each with its own command and expected outcome, and add an explicit `cargo check -p callisto-manifests --all-features` step before the coverage phase to catch any missing impl early. This will likely make T20 too large as a single 15-minute task — split it into multiple tasks if needed (e.g. T20a for fmt/lint/test, T20b for audit/doc-check, T20c for wasm-check/coverage, or whatever grouping keeps each under 15 minutes).

6. **T15/T16's `chmod 0o555` failure injection is a no-op under root** (the only coverage for AC-011/AC-011b): the test process may run as uid 0 in CI (common in containers), where mode 0o555 does not block file creation, so `apply_version_plan` would succeed and the tests would fail their own assertion — a hard CI break on the only tests covering these two error criteria. FIX: add an early-return guard to both test bodies: after `chmod`, probe whether write access was actually blocked (e.g. attempt to create a small probe file in the now-read-only directory; if it succeeds, clean it up, restore permissions, and `return` early from the test rather than asserting) rather than assuming the chmod took effect. State the exact mechanism in each task's `failing_test` description so the implementer doesn't silently drop the guard.

7. **T01b's `covers_criteria` is an empty array**: it should be `["AC-001"]`, matching T01a, since its two tests (PackageJson and PyprojectToml) directly exercise the trait-implementation completeness AC-001 requires. FIX: set it and note in T01b's reasoning that AC-001 is jointly covered by T01a and T01b.

8. **T04 is too large (bundles 8 discrete edits across a ~1500-line file)**: strips both persist calls from `CargoToml::write_version`, renames `permit`→`_permit`, inserts persist calls at 5 existing test call sites, inserts a delicate 3-way-ordering pre-persist assertion into `write_version_pins_explicitly_on_workspace_inheriting_member`, and adds one new test. FIX: split into T04a (production edit: strip both persist call sites, rename to `_permit`, plus one new test proving write_version doesn't touch disk until persist is called — this carries the genuine red) and T04b (the five existing-test persist insertions plus the delicate pre-persist assertion in the workspace-inheriting test, with the exact surrounding lines quoted verbatim at each insertion point so the 3-way ordering constraint is mechanical, not just described in prose). Split AC-015 coverage across both new tasks as appropriate. Renumber/adjust dependent task references as needed.

After all 8 fixes, re-verify programmatically (write and run a quick Python/jq check, don't just eyeball it) that every acceptance criterion in the spec (AC-001 through AC-020 plus AC-011b, or however many exist — read the spec's actual acceptance_criteria array to get the authoritative list) still appears in at least one task's covers_criteria after the renumbering, with no duplicate task IDs. Overwrite the plan at the same path with the corrected plan@1 JSON.

Optionally add a positive precondition first (open the handle directly, assert `current_version()` returns `Ok` with the expected version) so the test proves it actually reached `write_version` rather than failing upstream.

Given the earlier apply.rs wiring tasks (T03, T04, already reviewed/approved), `apply_version_plan` already calls `handle.persist(permit)?` explicitly after `write_version`/`update_dependency_spec` — so from this point forward, `apply_version_plan`'s end-to-end behavior should be UNCHANGED by this commit (it was already calling persist explicitly; now write_version just stops ALSO persisting internally, removing what was a redundant second write). 4. **Test quality**: verify all 5 repaired tests' persist() insertions are positioned correctly (before the disk read they're paired with, not accidentally before some other read), and that the new `write_version_does_not_touch_disk_until_persist_called` test is genuinely meaningful (checks disk BEFORE persist, then again AFTER).

# canon — Specification Skill

<overview>
canon turns requirements and research reports into unambiguous, testable specifications,
and turns defect class findings into architectural remediation specs. It enforces one
standard throughout: a developer who reads the output spec must be able to write an
implementation without asking a single clarifying question, and every acceptance
criterion must translate directly to a test case or type-level invariant check.
</overview>

---

<sub_skills>

### canon/draft
Given a `requirement@1` and optionally a `research-report@1`, produce a `spec@1` draft
with purpose, scope, non_goals, api_surface (if applicable), and acceptance criteria.
All criteria are testable propositions; error cases are covered with `is_error_case: true`.

### canon/verify
Given a draft `spec@1` plus the originating `requirement@1` and optional `research-report@1`, check whether each acceptance criterion is grounded in the source artifacts. Classifies criteria as supported, unsupported, or overfitted. Collects evidence only — does not produce a pass/fail verdict. Use this **before implementation** to confirm the spec is traceable to requirements.

### canon/drift
Given a spec@1 (via `spec_file_path`) and a workspace root, verify that the current code implements every acceptance criterion. Reads the spec from disk, reads the implementation from the workspace, and reports: `covered` (criterion is implemented and tested), `uncovered` (criterion has no matching implementation), and `drifted` (implementation exists but diverges from the criterion's contract). Use this **after implementation** to catch spec drift during maintenance — it is a diagnostic tool, not a blocking gate. lambda-exit-gate is the blocking gate; canon/drift is the ongoing health check.

### canon/audit
Given a `spec@1`, adversarially review it for untestable criteria, ambiguous language,
missing error cases, scope overlap, and incomplete sections. Returns a structured issue
list with specific rewritten suggested fixes.

### canon/gate
Given a `spec@1`, produce a binding pass/fail verdict before the spec enters planning. Default disposition is fail. On fail, returns specific blockers the drafter can act on without asking a follow-up question. On pass, the calling agent writes the spec to disk and sets `spec_file_path` — see the `<orchestration>` section.

### canon/architect
Given a `finding-report@1` from proof, produce a `spec@1` for the structural change that
eliminates the defect class — not a patch of individual instances but the abstraction
boundary, type invariant, or interface redesign that makes the class impossible to
reintroduce. This sub-skill closes the proof-to-design loop.

</sub_skills>

---

<artifact_contracts>

**Consumes**: `requirement@1`, `research-report@1` (optional), `finding-report@1` (canon/architect only), `spec_file_path` + workspace root (canon/drift only)

**Produces**: `spec@1` (written to `.claude/specs/<id>.json` by the skill orchestrator after gate pass; `spec_file_path` set to the workspace-relative path), `verdict@1` (canon/gate only)

</artifact_contracts>

---

<pipeline>

**Standard drafting pipeline:**
```
requirement@1 [+ research-report@1]
  → canon-drafter          (returns spec object — no disk write)
  → canon-verifier         (grounding check against source artifacts)
  → canon-auditor          (adversarial quality review)
  → canon-exit-gate        (binding pass/fail verdict)
  → [skill writes .claude/specs/<id>.json, sets spec_file_path]
  → spec@1
```

**On-demand drift pipeline (maintenance, any time after implementation):**
```
spec_file_path + workspace root
  → canon-drift-checker
  → drift report (covered / uncovered / drifted)
```

**Architectural remediation pipeline (invoked after proof):**
```
finding-report@1
  → canon-architect
  → canon-exit-gate
  → spec@1 (architectural)
  → vector → lambda
```

`canon-architect` is not part of the standard drafting pipeline. It is invoked when
proof returns a `finding-report@1` and the root cause requires a structural fix. The
output spec feeds back into vector for planning.

</pipeline>

---

<orchestration>

After `canon-exit-gate` returns a pass verdict, the calling agent MUST perform this step before handing off to vector:

1. Write the spec@1 JSON to `<workspace_root>/.claude/specs/<id>.json` using the file writing tool. Create the directory if it does not exist.
2. Set `spec_file_path` to the workspace-relative path (e.g. `.claude/specs/SPEC-001.json`) in the spec@1 object.
3. Pass the updated spec@1 — with `spec_file_path` set — to vector-planner.

This step is not optional. Without `spec_file_path` set, downstream agents fall back to reading the spec from conversation context, which is lossy under compression and cannot be independently verified.

</orchestration>

Requirement:
- crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs's apply_version_plan currently opens, reads, and parses a manifest file fresh (callisto_manifests::open) for EVERY entry in plan.bumps and plan.rewrites that targets it, and each of those calls Manifest::write_version / Manifest::update_dependency_spec internally persists (atomic_write: temp file + rename + fsync parent + fsync grandparent) on every single call. When N bumps/rewrites target the same file (e.g. an app crate depending on 5 sibling packages that bump together, all rewriting app/Cargo.toml's dependency table), this costs N full read+parse+write+2-fsync cycles on one file instead of 1.
- Confirmed via code reading: crates/callisto-manifests/src/{cargo,npm,python}.rs each implement the Manifest trait's write_version/update_dependency_spec/update_optional_dependencies by mutating an in-memory doc and then calling a private `fn persist(&mut self, permit: &ApplyPermit) -> Result<(), ManifestError>` at the end of every one of those methods.
- Fix requires: (1) restructure the Manifest trait (crates/callisto-manifests/src/lib.rs) so write_version/update_dependency_spec/update_optional_dependencies perform ONLY the in-memory mutation (no disk I/O), and expose persist as its own trait method the caller invokes explicitly; (2) apply.rs's apply_version_plan must group plan.bumps' writes and plan.rewrites by their resolved target path BEFORE looping, open each distinct path's manifest exactly once, apply every mutation destined for that path against the same open handle, then call persist() exactly once per file.
- Constraints to respect: CLAUDE.md invariant #2 (format preservation via CST editors) must hold across multiple in-memory mutations before the single persist. unsafe_code = "forbid" (workspace-wide). Must not silently change existing callers' expectations without updating them.
- Known blast radius to inventory precisely during spec/plan: ~28 existing call sites of write_version/update_dependency_spec/update_optional_dependencies inside crates/callisto-manifests/src/{cargo,npm,python}.rs's own #[cfg(test)] modules -- many read the manifest file back from disk immediately after calling one of these methods to assert on-disk content; each such test will need an explicit `.persist(&permit)` call added after its mutation(s) once auto-persist is removed. apply.rs itself is the only external (non-test) caller of these three methods anywhere in the workspace (confirmed via grep).
- Explicit design decision needed and must be captured as a testable acceptance criterion: partial-failure/atomicity semantics change. Today, if bump 3-of-5 fails validation (e.g. UnexpectedManifestVersion) mid-loop, bumps 1-2 have ALREADY been persisted to disk (partial application). After batching (mutate-all-in-memory-then-persist-once-per-file), a failure during in-memory mutation for a given file would mean NOTHING for that file gets persisted (that file's batch is all-or-nothing), while files whose batches completed successfully before the failing one would still be persisted (across-file atomicity is unchanged; per-file atomicity improves to all-or-nothing). This must be stated explicitly in the spec's acceptance criteria, not left implicit, and needs its own test.
- Out of scope: do not touch changelog writes, consumed-changeset deletion, pre.json write, or lockfile refresh logic in apply.rs -- only the plan.bumps (VersionWriteTarget::Manifest paths) and plan.rewrites (DepWriteTarget::Manifest paths) loops that currently call open()+write_version/update_dependency_spec per-entry. CargoWorkspacePackage/CargoWorkspaceDependency write targets (which go through WorkspaceCargoResolver, a different type, not the Manifest trait) are also out of scope for this track unless investigation shows they have the identical redundant-open problem -- check and note in the spec's scope section either way.

- axiom:axiom-exit-gate: Delegate to this subagent as the final step of the axiom gate protocol, after axiom-verifier has produced its verification report. Input is the verification report from axiom-verifier. The agent issues a definitive pass or fail verdict on whether the artifact meets all its criteria. Pass requires zero unresolved failures — unverifiable criteria are treated as failures unless the caller explicitly waives them. On fail, each blocker must be specific and actionable enough for the producing agent to make a targeted fix without further clarification. The agent increments retry_count by one if provided in input. Output is a verdict@1 conforming to shared/schemas/verdict@1.json, including verdict, confidence, blockers, verdict_summary (max 300 characters), artifact_type, and retry_count. (Tools: All tools)

- axiom:axiom-recon: Delegate to this subagent at the start of the axiom gate protocol when an artifact must be inventoried before verification begins. Input is an artifact path or description. The agent determines the artifact type, locates it in the workspace, enumerates the criteria it must be verified against (derived from a linked spec or requirement, or from the artifact's own acceptance criteria section if none is linked), and identifies source files to cross-check during verification. This is purely mechanical discovery — the agent produces no pass/fail opinion. Output is a JSON manifest with artifact_type, artifact_path, criteria array, source_files array, and a reasoning scratchpad. Do not delegate here for judgment; route the manifest to axiom-verifier for criterion cross-reference. (Tools: All tools)

- axiom:axiom-verifier: Delegate to this subagent after axiom-recon has produced its artifact manifest, and before any final verdict is issued. Input is the recon manifest from axiom-recon, including the artifact path, criteria list, and source files. The agent reads the artifact and each source file and, for each criterion, collects concrete evidence that confirms or refutes it. Each criterion is classified as verified (positive evidence found), failed (evidence contradicts the criterion), or unverifiable (requires external context not accessible). Absence of a counter-example is not sufficient to classify a criterion as verified. This agent is a neutral evidence collector — it does not issue verdicts. Output is a JSON object with verified, failed, and unverifiable arrays. Route output to axiom-exit-gate for the final verdict. (Tools: All tools)

- bug-hunter: Adversarial codebase auditor for deep, read-only bug hunts — silent failures, spec-vs-code drift, ordering/staleness bugs, security/path-containment issues, and edge cases. Use proactively for "audit", "adversarial review", or "find bugs" requests. Does not edit files. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- canon:canon-architect: Delegate to this subagent when proof has produced a finding-report@1 and the defect class requires a structural fix — a change to the architecture, type system, interface boundary, or abstraction layer — rather than a patch of individual bug instances. Input is a finding-report@1. Output is a spec@1 conforming to shared/schemas/spec@1.json describing the structural change that would make the confirmed defect class impossible or unrepresentable, not merely documented or harder to introduce. Acceptance criteria must be falsifiable at the type or API level: a test or type check that fails if the architectural invariant is violated. This agent closes the proof-to-design loop: proof surfaces what is broken, canon-architect specifies the structure that prevents it from being broken again. The output spec feeds into vector for planning and lambda for implementation. This agent does not patch instances — if the finding calls for local patches only, it still designs the structural containment that prevents the class from recurring. (Tools: All tools)

- canon:canon-auditor: Delegate to this subagent when you need adversarial quality review of a spec@1 before it enters planning. Input is a spec@1 JSON object. The auditor checks five dimensions: untestable or vague acceptance criteria, ambiguous phrasing that admits two valid interpretations, missing error cases for nil, malformed, or out-of-range inputs, scope overlap with other workspace specs, and TBDs or incomplete sections. For every issue found it produces a specific suggested fix — not generic guidance but rewritten text. Output is a JSON object with an issues array (criterion_id, type, description, suggested_fix per issue) and an overall pass or fail verdict. The judgment standard is: can a developer implement this spec without asking a single clarifying question? This agent does not check whether the spec matches source artifacts — that is the verifier's role. The auditor checks whether the spec, taken on its own terms, is complete, unambiguous, and implementable. (Tools: All tools)

- canon:canon-drafter: Delegate to this subagent when you have a completed requirement@1 and need a formal spec@1 drafted. Input is a requirement@1 JSON object and optionally a research-report@1. Output is a spec@1 conforming to shared/schemas/spec@1.json with id (SPEC-NNN matching the requirement id), purpose, scope, non_goals (at least one), acceptance_criteria (at least one), and optional api_surface if the feature has a callable interface. Every acceptance criterion must be a falsifiable proposition — confirmable true or false by a tester who has never seen the implementation, using only observable system behavior. No internal implementation knowledge may be required to check it. Error cases must carry is_error_case: true. Genuinely unknown items go in non_goals or the reasoning scratchpad — no TBDs are permitted anywhere. The reasoning field is private and never forwarded downstream. The canon skill orchestrator writes the spec to disk after canon-exit-gate passes — this agent returns the spec object only. (Tools: All tools)

- canon:canon-drift-checker: On-demand diagnostic: given a spec_file_path and a workspace root, verify that the current code still implements every acceptance criterion in the spec. Reads the spec from disk at spec_file_path — not from context. Reads the implementation and tests from the workspace. Classifies each criterion as: covered (implementation exists and tests assert the criterion's exact contract), uncovered (no corresponding implementation or test found), or drifted (implementation exists but the actual observable behavior diverges from what the criterion specifies). This is not a blocking gate — lambda-exit-gate is the blocking gate. Use this for ongoing maintenance to detect spec drift weeks or months after implementation, when the exit gate is long past. Output is a drift report with covered, uncovered, and drifted arrays plus a summary. (Tools: All tools)

- canon:canon-exit-gate: Delegate to this subagent when a spec@1 needs a definitive pass/fail judgment before entering the planning phase. Input is a spec@1 JSON object. This is an adversarial gatekeeper — the default disposition is fail, and the spec must earn a pass. The spec passes only if all four conditions hold: every acceptance criterion is a testable proposition with no vague language, no TBDs remain anywhere in the document, error cases are explicitly covered with is_error_case: true criteria, and the scope is narrow enough for a single planning cycle. On fail, every blocker is specific enough for the drafter to make a targeted fix without further clarification. Output is a verdict@1 conforming to shared/schemas/verdict@1.json with artifact_type set to spec@1. This agent is the binding exit gate — its fail verdict halts progression to vector until the spec is corrected and resubmitted. Maximum 3 retries before escalation to a human reviewer. (Tools: All tools)

- canon:canon-verifier: Delegate to this subagent when you need to verify that a draft spec@1 is grounded in its source artifacts — the requirement@1 and optional research-report@1 — before it proceeds to auditing or gating. Input is a spec@1 draft plus the originating requirement@1 and any research-report@1 used to produce it. For each acceptance criterion, the agent checks whether the requirement or research report supplies evidence that the criterion is necessary and correctly scoped. Each criterion is classified as supported (evidence found with a direct citation), unsupported (criterion appears with no basis in the source artifacts), or overfitted (criterion is narrower than the source supports, excluding valid cases). The agent collects evidence only and does not produce a pass/fail verdict. Output is a structured evidence report with supported, unsupported, and overfitted arrays plus a reasoning scratchpad. For post-implementation drift checking, use canon-drift-checker instead. (Tools: All tools)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- delta:delta-changeset-analyzer: Delegate to this subagent when you need a changeset@1 artifact produced from a git diff. Input is a git diff (readable via the git diff tool) and optionally a linked spec@1. The agent identifies files changed, detects breaking changes (public API removals, signature changes, behavior inversions), and maps which acceptance_criteria IDs from the linked spec are addressed by this diff. If no spec is linked, acceptance_criteria_met is set to unlinked. The summary is written in user-facing language (max 200 characters) describing what changed for a user, not an implementer. The agent reads shared/references/changesets.md for additional conventions and puts semver impact analysis in the reasoning scratchpad. Output is a changeset@1 conforming to shared/schemas/changeset@1.json. (Tools: All tools)

- delta:delta-commit-analyzer: Delegate to this subagent when the user has staged git changes and needs a conventional commit message written. Input is the staged diff, readable via the git diff tool. The agent reads shared/references/conventional-commits.md for type and scope conventions. Output is a JSON object containing commit_message, type (feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore, perf, ci, or build), scope (or null), a breaking flag, and a reasoning scratchpad. The commit message explains why the change was made, not what changed — the diff already shows what changed. The reasoning field is a private scratchpad explaining type and scope selection; it is not forwarded downstream. Use this subagent instead of writing commit messages manually. (Tools: All tools)

- delta:delta-pr-narrator: Delegate to this subagent when the user needs a pull request title and body written for a set of staged or committed changes. Input is a git diff (readable via the git diff tool) and optionally a linked spec@1 or requirement@1. The agent reads the PR template from shared/references/github.md and writes from the reviewer's perspective — what does a reviewer with zero prior context need to know to approve this confidently? Output is a JSON object with title, body, labels, and a reasoning scratchpad. The body covers what changed, why it was needed, and how to verify correctness. It explains the change's purpose, not a summary of the diff. Labels are inferred from the change type. (Tools: All tools)

- delta:delta-release-summarizer: Delegate to this subagent when you need a release-artifact@1 generated from a collection of changeset@1 entries. Input is a list of changeset@1 JSON objects, a target version string, and a release date in YYYY-MM-DD format. The agent reads shared/references/changesets.md for semver bump decision rules, filters out internal-only entries (chore, refactor with no user impact), and writes each changeset summary in user-facing language. Each changeset entry is typed as breaking (when breaking_changes are present), feat, fix, docs, or chore. All breaking_changes strings from all input changesets are aggregated into the top-level breaking_changes array. The reasoning scratchpad contains formatted markdown release notes ready to paste into a GitHub release. Output is a release-artifact@1 conforming to shared/schemas/release-artifact@1.json. (Tools: All tools)

- delta:delta-review-preprocessor: Delegate to this subagent when the user has received pull request review comments and needs them parsed, categorized, and turned into a prioritized action plan. Input is the raw PR review comment text. The agent categorizes each comment as must-fix (blocks merge), suggestion (optional improvement), or question (needs clarification before anything can proceed). Results are grouped by file. For must-fix items, the agent identifies the exact file location and the specific change required — concrete, not vague. Output is a JSON object with must_fix (file, location, comment, required_change), suggestions (file, location, comment), questions (file, comment), a summary string, and a reasoning scratchpad. The goal is a prioritized response plan the implementer can act on immediately without re-reading the original comments. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- graph:graph-auditor: Delegate to this subagent when you need to cross-reference all open requirements against existing specs, plans, and implementation files in the workspace. Input is a list of open requirement@1 objects and access to the workspace. The agent searches for spec and implementation files that address each requirement's done_when criteria, inspects candidate matches for substance, and detects requirements with overlapping or identical core statements. Output is a structured audit report with a per-requirement status (covered, partial, missing, or duplicate), evidence supporting each determination, duplicate_of references where applicable, and a one-paragraph summary of overall backlog health. Does not modify any files — read-only inspection only. Use this before planning to prevent duplicate or redundant work. (Tools: All tools)

- graph:graph-clarifier: Delegate to this subagent when a requirement@1 draft from graph-intake needs review for missing or underspecified dimensions before a spec can be written. Input is a requirement@1 JSON object. The agent evaluates gaps in priority order: testability of done_when criteria, specificity of stakeholder, and explicitness of out_of_scope boundaries. It then either asks one focused clarifying question or, if all dimensions are complete, returns the finished requirement with out_of_scope fully populated. Never asks multiple questions at once — one question per invocation. Output is a JSON object with action (question or complete), question (or null), the current requirement, and reasoning. When action is complete, out_of_scope is populated with explicit scope boundaries. Route completed requirements to canon-drafter. (Tools: All tools)

- graph:graph-intake: Delegate to this subagent when you have a raw need statement in free text — a problem description, user story, or feature request — and need it converted into a structured requirement@1 draft. Input is unstructured text only; no schema is required from the caller. The agent infers id, statement, stakeholder, why, and done_when from the provided text without asking any clarifying questions. Fields that cannot be inferred are omitted; gaps are noted in the reasoning scratchpad. The out_of_scope field is intentionally left empty — populating it is the graph-clarifier's responsibility. Output is a flat requirement@1 JSON object conforming to shared/schemas/requirement@1.json. Every done_when criterion must be a testable proposition verifiable from outside the implementation. Route this output directly to graph-clarifier before writing a spec. (Tools: All tools)

- lambda:lambda-exit-gate: Delegate to this subagent after all implementation tasks in a plan@1 are complete and lambda-mutator has run. Input is the workspace manifest from lambda-recon (which carries spec_file_path) and the lambda-mutator report. This is an adversarial verifier: it reads the spec directly from disk at spec_file_path and reads the current code state from scratch — it does not inherit any context from the implementer or reviewer and does not trust spec content forwarded through the conversation. It verifies that every acceptance criterion is implemented and covered by tests, all tests pass, no sibling functions with the same pattern were missed, no regressions were introduced, and that lambda-mutator ran and either passed or was noted as unavailable. Default posture is fail — a clean verdict means the agent looked hard and found nothing, not that it assumed the work was done. Output is a verdict@1 conforming to shared/schemas/verdict@1.json. When the retry count for a blocker exceeds 3, the gate escalates to a human rather than cycling again. (Tools: All tools)

- lambda:lambda-implementer: Delegate to this subagent to execute exactly one task from a plan@1 via the full TDD cycle. Input is a single task object from a plan@1, a workspace manifest from lambda-recon, and optionally a list of precision_tests from lambda-mutator (surviving mutant killers that must pass). When spec_file_path is present in the workspace manifest, reads the acceptance criteria for the task's covers_criteria IDs directly from that file before writing any tests — not from context. The agent writes the failing test first, confirms the red phase, then writes the minimum implementation to make it pass, confirms green, and commits. Skipping the red phase is not allowed — a test that passes before implementation indicates a broken test and the agent stops. When precision_tests are supplied, they are written as additional failing tests before any implementation begins; they must all reach green before committing. Output is a JSON status object with task_id, status, steps_completed, test_result, commit_sha, and optional concerns. Scope is strictly one task. Do not batch tasks. (Tools: All tools)

- lambda:lambda-mutator: Delegate to this subagent after lambda-implementer commits and before lambda-exit-gate runs. Input is the workspace manifest from lambda-recon and the list of files touched by lambda-implementer in the current task cycle. The agent detects the workspace language (Cargo.toml → rust uses cargo-mutants; package.json → typescript/javascript uses Stryker), runs mutation testing scoped to the implemented files, and analyzes survivors. For each surviving mutant the agent identifies exactly which code path it exposes and designs a precision test that would kill it. When survivors are found, the precision tests are returned to lambda-implementer for a targeted TDD cycle before the exit gate proceeds. When the mutation tool is not available in the workspace, the agent reports tool_unavailable rather than blocking, and lambda-exit-gate records this as a coverage gap. Output is a structured report with survived_mutants, precision_tests, and a verdict of pass or fail. (Tools: All tools)

- lambda:lambda-recon: Delegate to this subagent at the very start of a lambda protocol execution, before any implementation code is written. Input is a plan@1, a workspace root path, and optionally a spec_file_path. The agent detects the primary language by inspecting root config files (Cargo.toml → rust; package.json → typescript/js), locates the test runner and build tool, runs the full test suite to confirm the baseline passes, and inventories the files named in the plan. If baseline tests are failing the agent stops immediately — implementers must not start on a broken baseline. When spec_file_path is provided, the agent verifies the file exists and includes spec_file_path in the manifest; when absent or unreadable, it records a spec_file_warning in the manifest rather than failing. Output is a JSON workspace manifest: workspace_root, language, test_runner, build_tool, baseline_tests_pass, live_modules, plan_entry_points, and spec_file_path (null with warning if not provided or file not found). This manifest is the authoritative context for all downstream lambda agents. Do not skip this step. (Tools: All tools)

- lambda:lambda-reviewer: Delegate to this subagent after a lambda-implementer task commits and before lambda-exit-gate runs. Input is the set of commits from a completed implementation task, the original task specification, and the workspace manifest (which carries the language field). The agent loads the language-specific hazards reference (rust-hazards for Rust, typescript-hazards for TypeScript/JavaScript) and reviews four dimensions: scope adherence (implementation does exactly what the task required, no more, no less), non-negotiable violations (language-specific anti-patterns from the loaded hazards reference), sibling gaps (adjacent functions with the same pattern that should have been touched but were not), and test quality (the test verifies specified behavior, not an implementation detail). The reviewer is neutral — it collects and categorizes findings but does not issue a pass/fail verdict. That judgment belongs to lambda-exit-gate. Output is a JSON object with status, a per-issue list, and sibling_gaps. (Tools: All tools)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- proof:proof-adversary: Invoke once per candidate after proof-scanner (and proof-boundary-tracer for T7 or T10 candidates). Never batch multiple candidates in a single invocation. Input is one candidate@1 entry and the proof-recon manifest; for T7 or T10 candidates, also receives the field survival map from proof-boundary-tracer. The agent reads actual code at the reported location, traces control flow from the trigger condition, and tries to construct a valid refutation — a guard, type constraint, early return, or caller precondition that prevents the bug from manifesting. The default assumption is refuted. Before evaluating any candidate in a session, the agent performs a one-time constitution sweep: checks for CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md at the workspace root and flags architectural invariants that have no machine-enforcing rule as Invisible Invariants findings. A candidate confirms only when no refutation can be constructed and a concrete failing scenario can be stated. Output is a finding-report@1 entry or an explicit dismissal with evidence. Confirmed findings conform to shared/schemas/finding-report@1.json. (Tools: All tools)

- proof:proof-boundary-tracer: Conditional agent invoked only when proof-scanner produces candidates classified as T7 (write-only fields or intent-capture discard) or T10 (error downgrade). The agent traces every field of the flagged struct or type from its construction site through all call sites, parameter passing, and subprocess argument assembly, to determine whether each field reaches an execution boundary — a network call, subprocess invocation, storage write, or rendered output. Input is a finding-report@1 conforming to shared/schemas/finding-report@1.json plus a retry_count indicating how many prior exit-gate passes have occurred. The agent reads all affected code from scratch without inheriting any context from prior agents or the remediator. For each confirmed finding, it re-reads the file at the reported location and verifies the bug is no longer present. It scans affected files for sibling functions exhibiting the same pattern — a sibling gap counts as a blocker. It then runs the workspace compile and test commands and verifies both pass cleanly. Output is a verdict@1 conforming to shared/schemas/verdict@1.json. When retry_count exceeds 3, the agent escalates to human rather than issuing another verdict. This agent detects the primary language by inspecting Cargo.toml (rust) or package.json (typescript or javascript) at the workspace root. It identifies entry points such as binary crates, main.ts, or exported index files, then traces imports and module declarations from each entry point to construct a live file set. Every workspace file not reachable from any entry point is classified as dead. Output is a structured JSON manifest containing workspace_root, language, live_files, dead_files, entry_points, and a confidence rating reflecting how complete the reachability trace is. All downstream agents must operate only on live_files from this manifest. This agent performs no analysis and emits no opinions — mechanical enumeration only. (Tools: All tools)

- proof:proof-scanner: Invoke after proof-recon has produced a workspace manifest. Input is the manifest from proof-recon (including live_files and language) and optionally a specific hazard focus category. For Rust, the agent loads shared/references/rust-hazards.md; for TypeScript or JavaScript, it loads shared/references/typescript-hazards.md. It applies hazard taxonomies T1-T10 and their grep patterns, scanning only files in live_files. For each pattern match the agent reads surrounding code to assess surface plausibility, then emits a candidate@1 entry. The agent performs no adversarial reasoning and makes no filtering decisions — every plausible match is emitted. Output is a flat list of candidate@1 entries conforming to shared/schemas/candidate@1.json. Candidates are routed to proof-boundary-tracer (for T7 and T10) or directly to proof-adversary for confirmation. Missing a match is a false negative the adversary can never recover. The agent reads every identified source and extracts findings relevant to the question, with a citation, confidence level (confirmed, likely, or assumed), and source attribution for each. Does not synthesize or recommend — extracts faithfully from what it reads. Sources that cannot be read are noted as unreadable rather than skipped. Output is a JSON object containing a findings array, a sources_read list, and a reasoning scratchpad noting contradictions or surprises. The agent maps where answers might live — existing specs, docs, manifests, codebase patterns, or external sources — and returns a structured research agenda that tells trace-reader exactly which sources to read. Does not read file contents; relevance is assessed from names and directory structure only. Output is a JSON object containing internal_sources, external_keywords, existing_implementations, scope, and a reasoning scratchpad. - trace:trace-risk-assessor: Delegate to this subagent when a proposed approach or research-report@1 needs risk review before a spec is written. Input is a proposed approach or research-report@1 JSON, optionally accompanied by context about the target environment. The agent identifies technical risks that would materially affect the spec or plan if left unaddressed. For each risk it produces a description, severity (critical, high, medium, or low), likelihood, a concrete trigger condition describing when the risk materializes, and a mitigation sketch. Only risks with a plausible failure path are included — theoretical concerns without a realistic trigger are excluded. Output is a JSON object with a prioritized risks array and an overall_risk assessment. Surfaces risks neutrally — no recommendation about whether to proceed. (Tools: All tools)

- trace:trace-synthesizer: Delegate to this subagent after trace-reader produces a findings list. Input is the findings array and reasoning from trace-reader, along with the original research question. The agent synthesizes findings into a coherent research-report@1, surfaces contradictions between sources, identifies patterns across findings, and lists open questions that remain unanswered. Output is a complete research-report@1 conforming to shared/schemas/research-report@1.json. The recommendation includes an explicit confidence level (high, medium, or low), the rationale, a list of open questions, and any contradictions called out explicitly. Does not resolve contradictions by choosing a side without evidence — accuracy over tidiness. Route output to canon. (Tools: All tools)

Input is a plan@1 JSON object and its source spec@1 (read from spec_file_path if set). content.subject: Close gap 3: probe_git/check_git_version wiring
content.description: crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/git.rs:1-13 probe_git (never called anywhere). Investigated wiring options: no single funnel point exists (5+ independent GitAccess::discover call sites), GitAccess::discover is documented "Never fails" (breaking to make fallible), no actual git flag in shell.rs/access.rs requires >=2.20. Adversarial review caught this was wrong — docs/01-spec.md (§8, §C.6, §G.9.2, §G.10.1) and docs/00-design.md (§8) specify this feature in detail: separate git-ref namespace for Auto-trigger inference idempotency during pre-release cycles. ---
name: feedback-reviewer-must-actually-run-checks
description: lambda-reviewer and similar review agents sometimes self-report a check (e.g. "clippy clean") as passed without actually executing it; review prompts must explicitly demand real command execution and reading real output.
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

When dispatching a `lambda:lambda-reviewer` (or any adversarial review agent) to check something mechanical like `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`, do not trust a bare "clean, no warnings" claim in its report — during the SPEC-MANIFEST-PERSIST-001 track ([[project_manifest_persist_track]]), one reviewer (T15's review) reported clippy as clean when a real, live `needless_borrow` violation existed in the exact code it had just reviewed. The violation was only caught by the next task's reviewer, who was explicitly instructed to distrust the prior "clean" report and actually run the command.

**Why:** Agents can pattern-match "this is the kind of task where clippy is usually clean" and report success without invoking the tool, especially for tasks explicitly marked as having no production code change (which primes an expectation of "nothing to find here"). This is a silent-failure risk identical in shape to the kind of bug this codebase's own `bug-hunter`/`proof` agents hunt for in application code.

**How to apply:** When a review task involves a command-line check (clippy, tests, fmt, doc build), explicitly instruct the reviewer agent to "actually run `<command>` yourself and read the real output — do not just report clean based on inference." Once a false-clean report has happened in a track, call it out explicitly by name in every subsequent review prompt in that track ("a prior reviewer falsely reported X as clean — do not repeat that mistake") until the track ships. This pattern generalizes beyond clippy: any binary pass/fail claim from a review agent (tests pass, doc builds clean, no regressions) should be treated as unverified until the agent's own transcript shows the actual command output, not just its summary.

- `WorkspaceCargoResolver::write_version`/`write_dependency` still do combined mutate+persist in one call (never split like `Manifest` was in Spec A) — `cargo.rs:611-721`.
- The dual-targeting collision is real and reachable: a workspace root `Cargo.toml` that has one plain dependency and one `workspace = true` dependency produces, in the same `plan.rewrites`, both a `DepWriteTarget::Manifest("Cargo.toml")` entry (routed through the batchable `Manifest` trait) and a `DepWriteTarget::CargoWorkspaceDependency` entry targeting the same physical file (routed through `WorkspaceCargoResolver`'s separate, immediate read-modify-write). Today they're safe only because nothing is batched — each write is self-contained and sequential.
- `VersionWriteTarget::CargoWorkspacePackage` (the version-bump equivalent) has no production constructor anywhere — it's dead code today, so the version side of this collision is structurally unreachable. Only the dependency-rewrite side is live.

So the design question Spec B has to answer explicitly: what happens to a file that receives writes through *both* routing mechanisms in the same `apply_version_plan` call, once the `Manifest`-routed side starts batching (open once, mutate many, persist once)?

questions.question: How should Spec B handle a file that receives writes through both the Manifest trait AND WorkspaceCargoResolver in the same apply call (e.g. a workspace root Cargo.toml with one plain dependency and one workspace-inherited dependency both being rewritten)?

options.label: Exclude mixed-routing files from batching (Recommended)
options.description: Only batch (group+single-persist) files where every write for that path routes through the Manifest trait. Files that also receive a WorkspaceCargoResolver write in the same call keep today's safe, unbatched, immediate-write behavior for ALL their entries. Lowest risk — the collision this hazard depends on is narrow (root Cargo.toml only) and doesn't touch the common motivating case (N sibling packages rewriting one shared dependent's manifest, always non-root). Smaller performance win only in that narrow mixed case.

options.label: Order writes so the resolver always goes first
options.description: For any file targeted by both mechanisms, run all WorkspaceCargoResolver writes to it before opening the batched Manifest handle, so the handle's initial read reflects the resolver's already-flushed bytes. Requires restructuring apply_version_plan's write ordering to be path-aware across both loops rather than two independent loops. Delivers the full performance win everywhere but is a more invasive control-flow change with more surface area for a subtle bug.

options.label: Give WorkspaceCargoResolver the same mutate/persist split as Manifest
options.description: Extend the Spec A pattern to WorkspaceCargoResolver itself, then unify both routing mechanisms under one grouping-by-path mechanism with a single persist per file regardless of which mechanism did the mutation. Eliminates the hazard architecturally rather than by ordering, but is the largest-scope option — touches a type that was explicitly out of scope for Spec A, and is closest in shape to the original combined spec that triggered the first escalation.

Context worth knowing: the original combined spec that tried to do both the mutate/persist split AND the batching in one shot hit a real, formally-escalated data-loss ordering bug and had to be split into two specs. This draft is deliberately scoped to a "safe MVP" for the batching half: it excludes any manifest path that receives writes through BOTH the Manifest trait (batchable) AND WorkspaceCargoResolver (a separate, non-batched type) from batching entirely, rather than trying to interleave/order the two mechanisms correctly. This scope decision was made explicitly by the user via a 3-option tradeoff (exclude mixed-routing paths vs. reorder writes vs. extend the mutate/persist split to WorkspaceCargoResolver too) — the user picked "exclude" as the lowest-risk option. Do not second-guess that scope decision itself, but DO check whether the spec's language correctly and unambiguously implements "exclude" (not some other behavior) throughout.

Check your five standard dimensions: untestable/vague acceptance criteria, ambiguous phrasing admitting two valid interpretations, missing error cases for nil/malformed/out-of-range inputs, scope overlap with SPEC-MANIFEST-PERSIST-001 or other workspace specs, and TBDs/incomplete sections.

Pay particular attention to:
1. The spec introduces a NEW pub(crate) function `classify_manifest_writes` and a NEW `ManifestWriteGroup` struct, plus NEW `persist_call_count`/`reset_persist_call_count` instrumentation. Are these api_surface entries precise enough that an implementer wouldn't need to guess at field types, ordering, or semantics?
2. AC-011 (determinism: bump-before-rewrites, rewrites-in-plan-order) is supposed to be proven via an "order-sensitive fixture" rather than a coincidentally order-insensitive one. Is the criterion's language actually precise enough to force an implementer to construct a genuinely order-sensitive test, or could a lazy implementer satisfy the literal wording with a weak fixture?
3. AC-004 and AC-012 both cover partial-failure scenarios (mid-group failure, cross-file failure-after-earlier-success). Do they overlap in a way that's redundant, or are they testing genuinely distinct scenarios? Is the "which path is processed first in iteration order" nondeterminism in AC-012 actually testable, or does it leave an implementer without a fixed thing to assert?
4. Every non_goals item — are any of them actually acceptance criteria in disguise (i.e., things that ARE decided and should be testable, wrongly parked in non_goals to dodge specificity)?
5. The api_surface's PathBuf-equality-based path matching (no filesystem canonicalization) for classify_manifest_writes — is this explicitly enough stated as a decided behavior (not a TBD) with a clear enough rationale, given that path-equality bugs (e.g. "./Cargo.toml" vs "Cargo.toml" not matching) could silently defeat the whole batching feature?

Output your standard JSON issues array (criterion_id, type, description, suggested_fix per issue) plus an overall pass/fail verdict.

Deliberately added non_goals item 6 (behavior undefined for two distinct PlannedBump entries targeting the identical manifest path) rather than inventing an untested resolution: the requirement's own phrasing ('the path's bump mutation, if any' -- singular) presumes at most one bump per path, and I found no evidence in cascade.rs or the requirement that this is planner-constructible; per this task's own instruction, a genuinely unknown item belongs in non_goals, not a TBD or a guessed default. Added AC-013 specifically to make the WorkspaceCargoResolver-untouched claim (out_of_scope items 1 and 2 in the source requirement) independently falsifiable rather than leaving it as an unverifiable scope statement -- a tester can read the four named code paths and confirm zero diff against the Spec-A-era baseline. Added AC-011 to make the bump-before-rewrites, rewrites-in-plan.rewrites-order determinism claim falsifiable through an order-sensitive fixture rather than a coincidentally-order-insensitive one, since a naive test (e.g. two rewrites that don't overlap in the fields they touch) would pass regardless of application order and would not actually verify the ordering guarantee.\n\n--- REVISION 2, addressing canon-auditor FAIL verdict (two blocking, two medium, one minor) ---\n\nBlocking issue 1 (ManifestWriteGroup silently dropping the version-precondition check): re-read apply.rs:75-106 fresh, confirmed still current (three-way branch: current==to -> skip, no write_version, no persist, still pushed to modified_paths; current==from -> write_version then persist; else -> return Err immediately, before modified_paths.push is ever reached for that entry). The prior ManifestWriteGroup description said the batched pass 'applies handle.write_version(bump.1, permit) first (if bump is Some)' with zero mention of this branch -- a literal read would unconditionally mutate+eventually-persist even in the skip case, breaking apply_is_idempotent_when_manifest_already_at_target_version (which asserts the manifest bytes stay at 1.1.0, unbumped) and spuriously incrementing persist_call_count in a case that must stay at zero. Rewrote ManifestWriteGroup's api_surface description to spell out the three-way branch explicitly, added an in-memory `mutated` flag to make explicit exactly when persist() is (and is not) called, and added AC-014 as the auditor requested: a batched-group bump-precondition-failure test, deliberately kept distinct from AC-004 because AC-004's failure point is a rewrite AFTER a successful in-memory write_version, while AC-014's failure point is the version-precondition check BEFORE any mutation (bump or rewrite) is attempted -- an implementation could satisfy one without the other, so both need independent test coverage.\n\nBlocking issue 2 (AC-012's false 'regardless of iteration order' claim): confirmed classify_manifest_writes.batched is typed BTreeMap<PathBuf, ManifestWriteGroup> (deterministic lexicographic iteration) and apply_version_plan propagates all manifest errors via `?` (immediate short-circuit on first Err, per the existing bumps-loop and rewrites-loop code, unchanged by this spec's restructuring). Given that, AC-012's original claim is only true when P1 sorts before P2 -- if P2 sorted first and failed, apply_version_plan would abort before ever reaching P1's group, so P1 would be untouched original content, not 'reflecting its already-successfully-persisted batch' as originally worded. Deleted the false claim, pinned the fixture to require P1 < P2 lexicographically by PathBuf, and made that ordering requirement explicit and mandatory in the criterion text (not left to implementer discretion) so a test author can't accidentally pick names in the wrong order and get a coincidentally-passing but non-representative test.\n\nMedium issue 1 (AC-011's weak-fixture loophole): removed the 'OR, at minimum, so that the final byte content is only correct under the specified sequencing' escape clause, which was circular (restated the requirement rather than forcing a self-verifying construction). Replaced with a mandatory self-referencing-pin requirement: the rewrite's new DepSpec value must be derived from the bump's own target_version string, so applying it out of order produces an assertably-wrong (stale-version) string rather than a coincidentally-identical one. Explicitly ruled out the disjoint-fields loophole the auditor identified (bump touching [package].version, rewrite touching an unrelated [dependencies] entry with an independently-chosen value) as non-satisfying.\n\nMedium issue 2 (classify_manifest_writes's PathBuf-equality decision under-justified) -- full investigation, reported here with file:line citations since the task required either a cited AC, a non_goals disclosure, or a normalization-step fix, and I was able to fully verify the invariant rather than falling back to the weaker options:\n  1. Found the two production call sites that build PlannedBump.writes' VersionWriteTarget::Manifest paths: crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/version.rs:117-121 and crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/snapshot.rs:82-87. Both push VersionWriteTarget::Manifest(decl.path.clone()) for `decl in &pkg.manifests` filtered to ManifestRole::Canonical.\n  2. Found the rewrite-side construction in crates/callisto-graph/src/cascade.rs:230-247: DepWriteTarget::Manifest(edge.from_manifest.clone()) when edge.inherited is false; DepWriteTarget::CargoWorkspaceDependency{root_manifest: edge.from_manifest.clone()} when edge.inherited is true.\n  3. Traced edge.from_manifest's construction in crates/callisto-graph/src/walk.rs:336-374 (the ONLY production constructor of DepEdge, confirmed via `grep -rn 'from_manifest' crates/callisto-graph/src crates/callisto-model/src` -- the only other hits were test fixtures in cascade.rs and crosscheck.rs). For a non-inherited entry (the DepWriteTarget::Manifest case), declaring_path = decl.path.clone() at walk.rs:357 -- the SAME field, from the SAME `pkg.manifests` BTreeMap<PackageId, Package> (confirmed via resolver.rs:27-56: ManifestWalkResolver.packages backs BOTH DependencyResolver::packages() used by version.rs/snapshot.rs AND the `packages` map walk.rs iterates to build edges -- literally one shared map, not two independently-loaded copies), so for a package's own non-inherited manifest, the bump-write path and the rewrite-write path are not just equal by convention but are clones of the identical ManifestDecl.path field. No residual risk here.\n  4. The harder case is the inherited branch (declaring_path = inherited_dep.declared_in.to_path_buf() at walk.rs:348, a DIFFERENT source: WorkspaceInheritance.root_manifest, from crates/callisto-manifests/src/cargo.rs:502-509). Traced WorkspaceCargoResolver::load (cargo.rs:525-536): for an absolute input path it takes root_manifest_path.file_name() (discarding all directory components); for a relative input it calls workspace_relative(root_manifest_path) (full lexical normalization, preserving directory structure). These two branches would DIVERGE for a nested manifest path -- but grepped every production call site (`grep -rn 'WorkspaceCargoResolver::load'`) and confirmed all five non-test call sites (apply.rs:56,100,125; lib.rs:135; walk.rs:36) invoke it ONLY as WorkspaceCargoResolver::load(&root.join(\"Cargo.toml\")) -- always the literal workspace-root file, never a nested/member manifest. For that one call pattern, both branches converge to the same value: .file_name() of a root.join(\"Cargo.toml\") path trivially yields \"Cargo.toml\"; workspace_relative(root.join(\"Cargo.toml\")) also yields \"Cargo.toml\" once root itself is stripped, since workspace_relative lexically discards leading CurDir components (crates/callisto-model/src/path.rs:34, `Component::CurDir => {}`). So WorkspaceCargoResolver's root_manifest is always exactly PathBuf::from(\"Cargo.toml\"), no leading \"./\", no directory prefix -- for every real call site in this codebase.\n  5. Then checked the OTHER side of the comparison: what decl.path is for the workspace ROOT package's own canonical manifest (needed to confirm a root package's own VersionWriteTarget::Manifest bump-path matches root_manifest for AC-005/AC-006-style mixed-routing detection to work on the root file itself). Traced crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/ignore_walk.rs:145-161 (to_workspace_relative): for the workspace root specifically, path.strip_prefix(root) is empty, and the function explicitly returns PathBuf::from(\".\") (a literal dot) rather than an empty PathBuf. Traced walk.rs:64-95: manifest_rel = rel_path.join(filename) = PathBuf::from(\".\").join(\"Cargo.toml\") = PathBuf::from(\"./Cargo.toml\") -- WITH a leading dot -- which then gets passed into ManifestDecl::new(manifest_rel.clone(), ...) at walk.rs:93-95. My first pass through this chain concluded a real divergence (\"./Cargo.toml\" vs \"Cargo.toml\"); re-checking ManifestDecl::new itself (crates/callisto-model/src/package.rs:88-113) showed it calls workspace_relative(path) internally (package.rs:94) BEFORE storing the path -- and workspace_relative's CurDir-skipping normalization (path.rs:34, the same logic verified in step 4) strips that leading \".\" component during construction. So the FINAL decl.path stored in ManifestDecl for the root package is PathBuf::from(\"Cargo.toml\") -- no dot -- identical to WorkspaceCargoResolver's root_manifest value from step 4.\n  6. Net finding: the two independent normalization paths (ManifestDecl::new's explicit workspace_relative call, and WorkspaceCargoResolver::load's file_name()-or-workspace_relative branch) converge on the identical literal value PathBuf::from(\"Cargo.toml\") for the workspace root manifest, for every production call site that exists today. This is a genuine, verified invariant, not an assumption -- but it is NOT structurally guaranteed by the type system (it holds because of how these independent code paths happen to be called today, e.g. WorkspaceCargoResolver::load never being invoked with a nested path in production). Per the task's instruction to add a cited, falsifiable AC when verification succeeds, added AC-015: a new WorkspaceCargoResolver unit test (in cargo.rs, alongside its existing tests) plus a companion ManifestDecl::new assertion, both compared against PathBuf::from(\"Cargo.toml\"), so future changes to either normalization path (e.g. someone changing WorkspaceCargoResolver::load to preserve directory components, or someone changing to_workspace_relative to return an empty PathBuf instead of \".\") will fail this test rather than silently reintroducing the mixed-routing detection gap I initially (and incorrectly, before checking ManifestDecl::new's own normalization) suspected. message.content:
Another Claude session sent a message:
<teammate-message teammate_id="specb-auditor" color="green" summary="Re-audit: 3/4 fixes closed, 1 new blocking issue found">
Re-read the revised spec fresh (not the cached version — the Read tool initially returned a stale cache; I confirmed via file size/mtime and pulled raw content to be sure I was reviewing the actual current file). Verdict: **FAIL**, but real progress — 3 of the 4 original issues are genuinely closed, and I found one new blocking issue in the fix for issue 1, plus one trivial nit in AC-015.

## Original issues — verified status

**Blocking issue 1 (version-precondition check) — MOSTLY CLOSED, but see new finding below.** Re-read apply.rs:75-97 directly: the three-way branch (current==to → skip, no write_version/persist; current==from → write_version+persist; else → Err(UnexpectedManifestVersion) before modified_paths.push) is exactly as the revision describes. AC-014 is well-formed: testable, unambiguous, correctly distinct from AC-004 (bump-precondition failure BEFORE any mutation vs. rewrite failure AFTER a successful bump mutation — these really do exercise different code paths, good catch keeping them separate). However, the same paragraph introduces a new bug — see "NEW BLOCKING ISSUE" below.

**Blocking issue 2 (AC-012 false "regardless of order") — CLOSED.** Confirmed `classify_manifest_writes` returns `BTreeMap<PathBuf, ManifestWriteGroup>` (deterministic lexicographic iteration) and `apply_version_plan` still short-circuits via `?`. AC-012 now correctly pins P1 < P2 lexicographically and ties the claim explicitly to that ordering. No remaining inconsistency.

**Medium issue 1 (AC-011 weak-fixture loophole) — CLOSED.** The circular "OR, at minimum" clause is gone; the self-referencing-pin construction is now mandatory, and the disjoint-fields fixture is explicitly named and ruled out. Closes the loophole.

**Medium issue 2 (PathBuf-equality justification / AC-015) — CLOSED, independently re-traced end-to-end, not just trusted:**
- `commands/version.rs:117-121` and `commands/snapshot.rs:82-87`: confirmed both push `VersionWriteTarget::Manifest(decl.path.clone())` for canonical manifests.
- `cascade.rs:242-246`: confirmed `DepWriteTarget::CargoWorkspaceDependency{root_manifest: edge.from_manifest.clone()}` / `DepWriteTarget::Manifest(edge.from_manifest.clone())`.
- `walk.rs:336-374`: confirmed the ONLY production `DepEdge` constructor (grepped `from_manifest` across callisto-graph/callisto-model — only other hits are test fixtures in cascade.rs/crosscheck.rs). Confirmed `declaring_path` is `inherited_dep.declared_in.to_path_buf()` for inherited entries and `decl.path.clone()` otherwise — same field cascade.rs's non-inherited branch also uses.
- `callisto-manifests/cargo.rs`: confirmed `WorkspaceInheritance.root_manifest = self.root_path.clone()`, and `WorkspaceCargoResolver::load`'s two branches (`file_name()` for absolute input, `workspace_relative()` for relative) both reduce to `"Cargo.toml"` when called as `root.join("Cargo.toml")`.
- `locate/ignore_walk.rs:145-161`: confirmed `to_workspace_relative` returns `PathBuf::from(".")` exactly for the workspace root.
- `callisto-model/path.rs:34` / `package.rs:94`: confirmed `ManifestDecl::new` calls `workspace_relative`, whose `Component::CurDir => {}` arm silently drops leading `.` components — so `"./Cargo.toml"` normalizes to `"Cargo.toml"`, matching `WorkspaceCargoResolver`'s value exactly.
This is a genuinely correct, well-verified invariant and AC-015 is a solid regression test for it.
- **One minor, non-blocking inaccuracy**: AC-015's own criterion text claims `WorkspaceCargoResolver::load` is "called only ever as `WorkspaceCargoResolver::load(&root.join(\"Cargo.toml\"))`" at 5 named sites. I grepped and found 2 more production call sites the citation omits: `commands/publish_client.rs:239` (`self.cwd.join("Cargo.toml")`) and `callisto-manifests/cargo.rs:314` (`self.workspace_root.join("Cargo.toml")`). Both are harmless to the actual invariant — neither calls `.inheritance()` (one calls `.workspace_version()`, the other `.write_dependency()` directly), so neither ever produces a `root_manifest` value that feeds `classify_manifest_writes`'s comparison. But the criterion's literal enumeration is incomplete/inaccurate as written. Low severity, easy fix: narrow the claim to "every production call site that proceeds to call `.inheritance()`" and name those 3 sites specifically, rather than claiming it's the universe of all `WorkspaceCargoResolver::load` call sites.

## NEW BLOCKING ISSUE (introduced by this revision)

**`ManifestWriteGroup`'s persist-trigger condition is ambiguously worded, and its most natural literal reading silently drops a successful rewrite's mutation from disk.**

The api_surface text says: *"Only if `mutated` is true after the bump step and every rewrite in rewrite_indices has succeeded does the pass call handle.persist(permit)"*

But `mutated` is described as a cumulative flag that can be set true in TWO places: during the bump step (`current == from` → `write_version` called, `mutated = true`) AND during the rewrite step (*"calling handle.update_dependency_spec(...) for each and setting `mutated` true on the first one applied"*). The rewrite's in-memory mutation would be silently lost, never written to disk. This is a real correctness regression, not just an inefficiency, and it's exactly the class of silent-data-loss bug that caused the original combined spec to be split into two in the first place.

But the fix for blocking issue 1 introduced a new, higher-stakes ambiguity in the same mechanism, with a plausible real-world trigger (skip-bump + pending rewrites) and zero test coverage to catch a wrong implementation. Given this spec's whole reason for existing is a prior data-loss-from-ordering bug, I'd want this specific gap closed and back-verified before it moves to planning.
